messages.content: I want to infer directed cell–cell signaling from spatial transcriptomics, but nearby cells may share a microenvironment, and the relevant molecules may not all be observed. How should the goal be framed?

The goal is to distinguish a directed signaling explanation—one cell influencing another—from an explanation in which both cells respond to a shared microenvironment. Spatial proximity and associated expression patterns alone do not necessarily distinguish those possibilities, particularly under incomplete molecular observation. The inference should therefore include an account of when direction is identifiable and a way to flag cases where signaling and environmental explanations are observationally indistinguishable.
What does “observationally indistinguishable” mean here?

It means the available observations could be consistent with either explanation. A pattern attributed to signaling from one cell to another might also arise if both respond to an environmental influence that is not adequately observed. In that situation, the data do not justify presenting the directed signaling edge as uniquely determined. Flagging the ambiguity is different from concluding that signaling is absent or that the environment is definitely the cause.
So is the task just to find cells with related expression patterns at nearby locations?

No. Related patterns and spatial proximity may motivate a candidate relationship, but they do not by themselves establish a directed signaling edge. The task asks for directed cell–cell signaling inference while distinguishing it from shared-microenvironment effects. That distinction is central, not an optional qualification added after finding associations.
What needs to be said about identifiability?

The identifiability assumptions need to be explicit: under what conditions would the observations distinguish a directed effect from a shared environmental explanation, and under what conditions would they distinguish its direction? Those assumptions also need to acknowledge incomplete molecular observation rather than quietly treating every relevant influence as measured. Where the required distinction cannot be made, the result should be marked as ambiguous instead of stated as an identified directed edge.
Can an assumption make an edge identifiable even though some molecules are missing?

Potentially, but that would depend on what the assumption supplies and whether it is defensible for the inference being made. Incomplete molecular observation does not automatically make every edge unidentifiable; nor does an assumption automatically remove the possibility that an unobserved influence mimics signaling. The important point is to state what information or restrictions permit the distinction and to limit any directional claim to the cases those conditions cover.
I also want a concrete performance target. What is it?

On synthetic confounded tissues, the target is at least 80% precision at 50% recall for identifiable directed signaling edges. It is a target to achieve, not a result already established. The qualification “identifiable” matters: the stated performance target concerns directed edges for which the available setup permits a distinction, while observationally indistinguishable signaling and environmental explanations still need to be flagged.
How should I read “80% precision at 50% recall” without losing the directed-edge part?

Among edges called as directed signaling edges at the operating point that attains 50% recall, at least 80% should be correct. Recall refers to recovering 50% of the identifiable directed signaling edges against which that performance is assessed. Correctness includes the direction: identifying a relationship between two cells is not enough if the claimed sender-to-receiver direction is wrong.
Does the target mean the system has to assign a direction to every apparent interaction?

No. The goal explicitly requires flagging observationally indistinguishable signaling and environmental explanations. Assigning a confident direction in every apparent interaction would obscure that requirement. The precision-and-recall target applies to identifiable directed signaling edges on synthetic confounded tissues; it should not be read as a requirement to turn ambiguous observations into directional claims.
What role does “synthetic confounded tissues” play in that statement?

It specifies the setting for the performance target. The target is not merely to detect patterns in an uncomplicated spatial dataset; it is to reach at least 80% precision at 50% recall for identifiable directed signaling edges in synthetic tissues where confounding is part of the challenge. That setting is also why separating signaling from shared-microenvironment explanations matters.
Could we describe the entire objective without implying that the inference has already been demonstrated?

Yes: infer directed cell–cell signaling from spatial transcriptomics under incomplete molecular observation, explicitly state the assumptions needed to identify direction and distinguish signaling from shared-microenvironment effects, and flag cases where those explanations are observationally indistinguishable. The performance goal is to achieve at least 80% precision at 50% recall for identifiable directed signaling edges on synthetic confounded tissues. That wording states the objective and its testable target without claiming the target has already been met.
What approach would you propose for separating directed signaling from shared-microenvironment effects?

Develop SignalSep: a masked ligand–receptor spatial model with latent environmental factors and observational-equivalence checks. The ligand–receptor component addresses candidate cell–cell signaling, while the latent factors allow for shared environmental influences. The equivalence checks are there to identify cases where the observations cannot distinguish those explanations; SignalSep would abstain on directed edges that are unidentifiable.
Why include a mask in the ligand–receptor model?

Because the molecular observations are incomplete. A masked model can represent that limitation explicitly rather than treating every relevant molecule as though it had been observed. The proposal does not yet specify an exact masking rule or how missing molecular information would be handled computationally, so the mask should not be taken as a claim that the missing information can be recovered.
What does the spatial part contribute?

It keeps the inference tied to the spatial transcriptomics setting, where the locations of cells are part of the observations. But spatial relationships do not, on their own, establish that one cell signaled to another. Nearby cells could instead exhibit related expression because they share a microenvironment. SignalSep is proposed to consider that alternative within the model rather than treating spatial association as a directed edge.
How do the latent environmental factors help with that distinction?

They provide a way to represent shared environmental influences that may not be directly observed. Without such an alternative in the model, a pattern shared by cells could be attributed too readily to cell–cell signaling. Including latent factors does not itself prove which explanation is correct; it makes the environmental explanation part of what the directed-edge claim has to contend with.
Are those latent factors supposed to correspond to particular measured molecules?

The proposal does not specify that. They are latent environmental factors, so they represent influences not directly observed in the stated model. It would be too strong to assign them particular molecular identities from this description alone, or to say that adding them makes all environmental confounding observable.
Then what is an observational-equivalence check meant to ask?

It asks whether the available observations distinguish a proposed directed signaling explanation from an alternative explanation, including a shared-environment one. If the alternatives are observationally indistinguishable, the check should prevent that candidate from being reported as an identified directed edge. The proposal names this check but does not prescribe a particular test or algorithm for carrying it out.
Is that different from just assigning a low confidence score to the edge?

Yes, conceptually. A low score might express weak evidence, whereas observational equivalence identifies a more specific limit: the observations cannot discriminate between explanations relevant to the directional claim. The proposed response to an unidentifiable directed edge is abstention, rather than making a directional call despite that ambiguity. No particular scoring scheme is specified here.
Does abstaining mean SignalSep has decided there is no signaling?

No. Abstention means it does not claim an identifiable directed edge from the available observations. Signaling might still be possible, but a shared-microenvironment explanation or another observationally equivalent account cannot be ruled out on the stated basis. That is a limit on the inference, not a finding that signaling is absent.
Suppose a ligand–receptor pattern looks compatible with signaling. Why not report the direction and add a caveat?

Compatibility is not the same as identification. If the pattern is also compatible with an environmental explanation that the observations cannot distinguish, reporting the direction as an inferred edge would overstate what the evidence supports. SignalSep’s proposed equivalence checks and abstention are intended to keep a plausible signaling story separate from an identifiable directed claim.
Would the checks also matter if the ambiguity is about which cell is the sender?

Yes. The claim at issue is a directed edge, so an inability to distinguish its direction is an identifiability problem too. The proposal calls for abstaining on unidentifiable directed edges; it does not limit abstention to cases where signaling and environment are the only competing explanations.
Does putting ligand–receptor information, spatial information, and latent factors together guarantee that the explanations become distinguishable?

No. Those components provide a proposed way to represent candidate signaling, spatial observations, and shared environmental effects. They do not guarantee that the available observations contain enough information to separate the explanations. That is precisely why the observational-equivalence checks and abstention are part of SignalSep rather than assuming every candidate can be assigned a direction.
Where do identifiability assumptions enter the proposal?

They are needed to interpret any directed edge that SignalSep does report. The model and its checks would have to make clear what assumptions let the observed pattern discriminate a directed signaling edge from environmental alternatives, especially with incomplete molecular observation. The current proposal does not spell out those assumptions in detail, so it should not be presented as already resolving every identifiability question.
Can I describe SignalSep as a method that discovers the true sender and receiver for every candidate pair?

That would conflict with the proposal. SignalSep is intended to infer directed edges only where they are identifiable under its stated assumptions and to abstain where the observations leave the direction or explanation unresolved. Its central distinction is between making a supported directional claim and recognizing that the same observed pattern admits an alternative account.
How would you state the proposal in one careful sentence?

Develop SignalSep, a masked ligand–receptor spatial model that accounts for latent environmental factors and uses observational-equivalence checks to abstain on directed cell–cell signaling edges that cannot be identified from the available observations.
Here is the question I want to pin down: when can a neighbor’s partially observed ligand profile distinguish directed signaling from an unmeasured niche factor affecting both cells?

Only when the available observations, together with explicit and defensible assumptions, can separate those explanations. A neighbor’s ligand profile may be compatible with the neighbor influencing another cell, but an unmeasured niche factor affecting both cells could also produce an association. Partial observation makes that distinction harder: what is unobserved cannot simply be treated as absent. The question is whether a common-niche explanation remains observationally equivalent to the proposed directed one.
If the neighbor expresses a ligand and the other cell shows a compatible response, isn't that enough to establish the direction?

Not necessarily. That pattern is compatible with the proposed direction, but compatibility alone does not establish it. An unmeasured niche factor could affect the neighbor’s observed ligand profile and the other cell’s observed state, yielding a similar pattern without the directed influence being identifiable. The question is what, if anything, in the observations or assumptions distinguishes those possibilities.
So the unmeasured factor isn't just noise in the other cell's response?

Right. In this question, the niche factor can affect both cells. It could therefore help explain why the neighbor’s ligand profile and the other cell’s state vary together. Treating it merely as unexplained variation in one cell would miss the common-cause alternative that makes the signaling inference difficult.
How does the ligand profile being only partially observed change what we can conclude?

It limits what the profile can rule out. An observed part of the profile may support a candidate signaling explanation, but missing molecular observations leave open possibilities that cannot be evaluated directly from that profile. A defensible answer has to distinguish ‘not observed’ from ‘observed not to be present’ and state whether the missing information affects the particular directional claim.
Does incomplete observation make every proposed signaling direction unidentifiable?

No automatic conclusion follows either way. Some directional claims might be distinguishable under suitable assumptions despite incomplete observation; others might remain observationally equivalent to a shared-niche account. The point of the question is to identify where that boundary lies, rather than presume that partial observation always permits or always prevents inference.
What would an identifiability assumption need to accomplish here?

It would need to justify why the observed association can be attributed to the proposed direction rather than equally well to an unmeasured niche factor affecting both cells. It would also need to address the relevant limits of the partially observed ligand profile. Merely stating that signaling is plausible would not do the work: the assumption has to support discrimination between the competing explanations.
Could spatial proximity settle it? The cells are neighbors.

Neighboring cells can plausibly interact, but they may also share a niche. Proximity is therefore relevant to both stories and does not, by itself, settle which one produced the observed pattern. The question remains whether there is a basis for distinguishing directed influence from that shared environmental effect.
What if the ligand and the other cell's state are strongly associated?

A strong association does not by itself resolve the ambiguity. If an unmeasured niche factor can affect both, it may also account for a strong association. Strength of association and identifiability are different issues: a clear pattern can still admit more than one explanation.
Is the issue whether the ligand is genuinely involved, or whether the neighbor caused the other cell's response?

The directed claim requires more than recognizing a ligand-related pattern. It says that the neighbor influenced the other cell in that direction. An unmeasured niche affecting both could leave a ligand profile that looks relevant without the observations distinguishing that directed influence from a common cause. The question asks when the partially observed profile can support the stronger claim.
If we cannot tell, should we label the niche factor as the cause instead?

No. Failure to distinguish the explanations is not evidence that the niche factor, rather than signaling, was the cause. It means the available basis does not identify which explanation accounts for the pattern. The appropriate characterization is ambiguity about the directed edge, not a confident switch to the environmental explanation.
How would this question relate to SignalSep's observational-equivalence checks?

It gives those checks their central challenge: determine whether a directed explanation involving the neighbor’s partially observed ligand profile can be distinguished from an unmeasured niche explanation affecting both cells. If the explanations remain observationally equivalent, SignalSep’s proposed response is to abstain on the unidentifiable directed edge. The question does not yet specify exactly how to perform the check or which assumptions would make it decisive.
Could the model's latent environmental factors automatically remove the ambiguity?

No. Representing latent environmental influences makes the alternative available for consideration; it does not guarantee that their effects can be separated from signaling in the observations. If a directed-signaling account and a shared-niche account still fit what is observed equally well for the purpose of the directional claim, the latent-factor representation alone does not identify the edge.
Then what is a careful answer to the question as it stands?

A neighbor’s partially observed ligand profile can distinguish directed signaling from an unmeasured niche factor affecting both cells only to the extent that explicit assumptions and the available observations rule out an observationally equivalent shared-niche explanation for that directed claim. If they cannot, the profile may motivate a signaling hypothesis, but it cannot identify the direction; the edge should remain flagged as ambiguous rather than asserted.

I have a hypothesis about the distinction: niche-independent variation in a sender’s ligand predicts receptor-linked responses in neighboring cells. But when the ligand and niche fields coincide, their effects are observationally indistinguishable. Is that the right way to state it?

Yes, as a hypothesis. It identifies a potential source of distinction—variation in the sender’s ligand that is independent of the niche—and a limit on that distinction: if the ligand and niche fields coincide, the observed pattern cannot separate their effects. It should not be phrased as though either part has already been demonstrated.
Why does the ligand variation have to be niche-independent?

Because the competing explanation is that the niche affects both cells. If the sender’s ligand varies only along with the niche, a receptor-linked response in a neighbor could track either the ligand-associated signaling explanation or the shared-niche explanation. Niche-independent ligand variation is the part of the hypothesis that could provide information for distinguishing them.
What does it mean to say that this variation ‘predicts’ a neighbor’s response?

In the hypothesis, differences in the sender’s ligand are expected to be informative about receptor-linked responses in neighboring cells, beyond what can be explained by the niche variation at issue. ‘Predicts’ describes an expected relationship; by itself, it does not establish that the ligand caused the response or that a particular directed edge is identifiable.
And why specify that the neighbor’s response is receptor-linked?

It connects the proposed response to the ligand–receptor signaling account, rather than treating any change in a neighboring cell as evidence for signaling. Even a receptor-linked pattern must be assessed against the shared-niche explanation. The phrase narrows what the hypothesis predicts; it does not make the niche alternative disappear.
If I observe that predicted pattern, can I call the sender-to-neighbor edge directed signaling?

Not on that observation alone. The hypothesis says niche-independent ligand variation could help distinguish the directed explanation. A directional claim still depends on whether the independence and the relevant distinction are supported under explicit assumptions, especially with incomplete molecular observation. If the observed pattern admits an equivalent niche explanation, the edge remains unidentifiable.
What exactly is meant by the ligand and niche fields ‘coinciding’?

The key point is that their observed spatial variation does not provide a basis for telling their effects apart. Where the ligand pattern and the niche pattern coincide, a neighbor’s response associated with that pattern can be attributed to either account without the observations distinguishing them. The hypothesis does not require treating every spatially associated ligand pattern as coincident with the niche; it identifies coincidence as the problematic case.
Could a very strong receptor-linked response solve the coincidence problem?

Not simply by being strong. If the ligand and niche fields coincide, the response may be strongly associated with their shared pattern while still leaving their effects observationally indistinguishable. The difficulty is not necessarily a weak pattern; it is the absence of variation that separates the two explanations.
Does ‘observationally indistinguishable’ mean the ligand has no effect when the fields coincide?

No. It means the observations cannot distinguish the ligand’s proposed effect from the niche effect in that circumstance. Signaling could be present, the niche could account for the response, or their contributions could be difficult to separate. The hypothesis concerns what can be inferred from the observations, not a finding that the ligand is inactive.
Would it be equally wrong to say the niche definitely caused the response?

Yes. Coincidence makes the explanations observationally indistinguishable; it does not select the niche explanation as the true one. A careful account would flag the ambiguity rather than make a confident causal claim in either direction.
Does this hypothesis answer the question about a partially observed ligand profile?

It proposes a conditional answer. A partially observed sender-ligand profile may help distinguish directed signaling when it contains informative variation independent of the niche and that variation predicts receptor-linked neighbor responses under the necessary assumptions. When the ligand and niche fields coincide, the proposed distinction is unavailable from those observations. Because the profile is only partially observed, neither independence nor the absence of a competing explanation should be assumed without qualification.
Is niche-independent variation the same thing as saying the two cells are in different locations?

No. Spatial location alone does not establish independence from the niche. The hypothesis concerns variation in the sender’s ligand that is separable from niche variation. Merely identifying locations or neighboring cells would not show that the ligand pattern provides that separation.
How does this connect to abstaining on unidentifiable edges?

The hypothesis gives a reason to look for distinguishable variation before making a directed claim. If ligand and niche fields coincide, their effects are observationally indistinguishable, so a directed edge should not be presented as identified on that basis. Abstention preserves the possibility of signaling without claiming that the available observations have separated it from the niche effect.
Is the proposed predictive relationship already an identifiability assumption?

It is part of the hypothesis about what could be informative, but it is not a complete identifiability argument by itself. One would still need to state the assumptions under which the ligand variation is genuinely niche-independent and the receptor-linked neighbor response distinguishes the directed account from an environmental one. Those conditions should not be silently inferred from a predictive association.
Can you give me a concise version that keeps both halves of the hypothesis together?

The hypothesis is that niche-independent variation in a sender’s ligand predicts receptor-linked responses in neighboring cells, providing a potential basis for distinguishing directed signaling; when ligand and niche fields coincide, however, their effects are observationally indistinguishable. The first half proposes a distinguishing pattern, and the second states a limit on what that pattern can identify.
How can we evaluate the hypothesis about niche-independent ligand variation without treating it as an established result?

Simulate NicheMix-1 tissues with 40% dropout, comparing ligand–niche correlations of 0.2 versus 1.0. Then assess SignalSep’s directed-edge recovery and its abstention in each condition. That sets up a test of whether the change in ligand–niche association affects what SignalSep can identify; it does not presume the outcome.
What is the purpose of comparing 0.2 with 1.0?

The two values create a contrast in how closely ligand and niche variation track one another. A ligand–niche correlation of 0.2 leaves more separation between those patterns than a correlation of 1.0, which denotes perfect correlation. The comparison probes the hypothesis that separable ligand variation can help distinguish directed signaling, whereas coincident patterns leave the signaling and niche explanations difficult or impossible to distinguish observationally.
Should I call the 0.2 condition niche-independent?

Not without qualification. A ligand–niche correlation of 0.2 is not zero, so it does not state that the ligand is independent of the niche. It specifies the lower-correlation condition in this comparison. The activity can ask whether that condition gives SignalSep more basis for recovering directed edges than the 1.0 condition, without claiming that 0.2 eliminates niche effects.
Does a correlation of 1.0 mean the ligand and niche fields have exactly the same values everywhere?

It establishes perfect correlation in the proposed comparison, not necessarily identical numerical values. What matters for the hypothesis is that perfectly aligned variation offers no separation along that dimension between the ligand and niche patterns. The simulation can assess whether SignalSep recognizes the resulting identifiability issue rather than forcing a directed-edge call.
Why keep dropout at 40% in both conditions?

The specified activity uses 40% dropout while varying the ligand–niche correlation between 0.2 and 1.0. Holding that stated level constant makes the comparison about the correlation contrast under the same stated degree of dropout. The activity does not specify a dropout mechanism, so it would be premature to describe exactly which observations are missing or how they are selected.
What should ‘edge recovery’ mean when we assess SignalSep?

It concerns whether SignalSep recovers the directed signaling edges that the simulated tissues allow us to assess, including their direction, rather than merely finding spatially associated cell pairs. The activity calls for assessing recovery but does not yet specify a particular metric or scoring procedure. Any report of recovery should keep an identified directed edge distinct from an association that remains compatible with a niche explanation.
And abstention is a separate part of the assessment?

Yes. SignalSep is proposed to abstain when a directed edge is unidentifiable. Assessing only recovered edges could miss whether it makes unjustified directional calls in ambiguous cases. Looking at abstention alongside edge recovery asks both whether it identifies edges when the observations permit that and whether it refrains from identifying them when the competing explanations cannot be distinguished.
Would more abstention at correlation 1.0 automatically count as success?

No. Greater abstention by itself does not show that SignalSep is making the right distinctions; a method could abstain indiscriminately. The assessment needs to consider abstention together with directed-edge recovery and the identifiability of the cases being assessed. The proposed activity does not assert that either correlation condition will produce a particular abstention rate.
What if it recovers many edges at correlation 1.0?

That would call for examining whether those directed edges are actually distinguishable from niche explanations under the simulation’s stated assumptions. A high number of calls alone would not resolve the question. The point of assessing abstention is to avoid interpreting every apparent edge as identified when ligand and niche variation may be observationally inseparable.
Does the activity prove that every edge in the 0.2 condition is identifiable and every edge in the 1.0 condition is not?

No. The correlation values describe a comparison between tissue conditions; they are not, by themselves, labels assigning identifiability to every individual edge. The evaluation should not equate lower correlation with guaranteed identification or perfect correlation with a fully specified conclusion about every possible observation. It tests how recovery and abstention behave across the contrast.
How does the 40% dropout relate to the original question about partially observed ligand profiles?

It places the simulated comparison under incomplete observation, so the assessment is not limited to a fully observed ligand profile. With 40% dropout stipulated, the question becomes whether SignalSep can recover directed edges and abstain appropriately despite that missing information. Nothing in the activity says that the dropped information can be reconstructed or that its absence has the same consequence for every edge.
What would be a mistaken interpretation of a ligand-associated neighbor response in these tissues?

It would be mistaken to treat the association alone as proof of directed signaling. The simulated tissues are meant to probe the possibility that niche variation affects what appears to be a ligand-linked neighbor response. Especially when ligand and niche patterns track each other closely, assessing whether SignalSep abstains is as important as counting directed edges it reports.
Do we have an outcome for NicheMix-1 yet?

No outcome is stated here. The activity is to simulate NicheMix-1 tissues at 40% dropout with ligand–niche correlations of 0.2 versus 1.0, then assess SignalSep edge recovery and abstention. Any statement that SignalSep has achieved a particular recovery or abstention result would go beyond this activity.
Can you phrase the evaluation plan compactly without suggesting it has already been run?

Simulate NicheMix-1 tissues with 40% dropout under ligand–niche correlations of 0.2 and 1.0, and compare SignalSep’s directed-edge recovery and abstention across the two conditions. Use the comparison to evaluate, rather than assume, whether separation between ligand and niche variation helps identify directed signaling and whether coincident variation prompts appropriate abstention.
What did the NicheMix-1 assessment show for SignalSep?

On NicheMix-1, SignalSep reached 84% precision at 50% recall in the ligand–niche correlation condition r=0.2. In the r=1.0 condition, it abstained on 96% of indistinguishable edges. Those are two different observations: one reports directed-edge recovery at a specified recall level, and the other reports abstention on edges whose explanations are indistinguishable.
How should I read the 84% figure?

It is precision at the operating point where recall is 50%, for the NicheMix-1 condition with r=0.2. In other words, 84% of the directed edges reported at that point were correct under the assessment, while recall was 50%. It is not a claim of 84% recall, or a precision figure for every possible operating point.
Does 50% recall mean SignalSep recovered half of all possible cell–cell interactions?

No. Recall concerns the directed edges used as the reference for this assessment, not every conceivable interaction between cells. The result gives a precision–recall point for SignalSep at r=0.2; it does not say that half of all possible cell pairs interact.
And what does the 96% figure measure?

At r=1.0, SignalSep abstained on 96% of the edges classified as indistinguishable in the assessment. That is an abstention result, not a precision or recall result. It indicates how often SignalSep withheld a directed claim for those indistinguishable edges in that condition.
Is the remaining 4% necessarily a set of false directed edges?

The reported 96% abstention leaves 4% of those indistinguishable edges outside the abstained group, but this statement does not specify how those cases were handled or scored. It would go beyond the result to label every one of them a false directed edge without further information.
Can I compare 84% and 96% directly as though they were the same metric?

No. The 84% is precision at 50% recall for r=0.2; the 96% is the fraction of indistinguishable edges on which SignalSep abstained for r=1.0. They describe different behaviors on different subsets and should retain their respective denominators and correlation conditions when reported.
Why does the correlation condition need to accompany each number?

Because the numbers answer different questions under different ligand–niche relationships. The edge-recovery figure is reported for r=0.2, whereas the abstention figure concerns indistinguishable edges at r=1.0. Omitting the conditions could make it sound as if both figures were measured on the same cases or applied uniformly across NicheMix-1.
Does the r=1.0 result establish that the niche, rather than signaling, caused those edges?

No. The edges are described as indistinguishable, meaning the available observations do not separate the directed-signaling and niche explanations for them. SignalSep’s abstention avoids choosing a direction on that basis; it is not a determination that the niche explanation is true.
What does the contrast between these results tell us, without overstating it?

In the reported NicheMix-1 assessment, SignalSep recovered directed edges with 84% precision at 50% recall when r=0.2, and withheld directed claims for 96% of indistinguishable edges when r=1.0. The contrast is relevant to the proposed distinction between ligand variation that can be separated from niche variation and variation that coincides with it. The figures do not, by themselves, establish that every edge at r=0.2 is identifiable or that every edge at r=1.0 is indistinguishable.
Could I say that perfect ligand–niche correlation made SignalSep abstain on 96% of all edges?

No. The stated denominator is indistinguishable edges at r=1.0, not all edges in that condition. Keeping that qualifier matters: 96% abstention on indistinguishable edges is a more specific finding than 96% abstention across every candidate edge.
Is 84% precision the same as saying SignalSep is generally 84% accurate?

No. Precision here describes the correctness of reported directed edges at 50% recall in the r=0.2 NicheMix-1 condition. It is not an overall accuracy measure and should not be generalized to other conditions or operating points from this result alone.
Does the result say anything about incomplete molecular observation?

The NicheMix-1 assessment was set up with 40% dropout, so these reported results come from that incomplete-observation setting. They do not establish how SignalSep would behave at other dropout levels or under other patterns of missing observations.
What would be the most careful short report of the evidence?

On NicheMix-1 with 40% dropout, SignalSep reached 84% precision at 50% recall for r=0.2 and abstained on 96% of indistinguishable edges for r=1.0. Report the first as an edge-recovery figure and the second as an abstention figure, without treating abstention as proof that signaling was absent.
Given the SignalSep evidence, what decision should we make?

Adopt SignalSep with abstention. Its 84% precision at 50% recall clears the stated precision target, while 96% of indistinguishable edges are flagged rather than treated as identified directed signaling edges. Both parts matter to the decision: recovering directed edges and recognizing when a directional claim is not justified.
How does 84% clear the target?

The target is at least 80% precision at 50% recall for identifiable directed signaling edges on synthetic confounded tissues. SignalSep reached 84% precision at 50% recall in the reported NicheMix-1 assessment, exceeding the precision threshold by four percentage points at that recall level. That is the basis for saying it clears the target; it is not a claim about every setting or recall level.
Does adopting it mean reporting every candidate ligand–receptor connection as a directed edge?

No. The decision specifically adopts SignalSep *with abstention*. A candidate may be compatible with signaling without being distinguishable from a shared-microenvironment explanation. For an unidentifiable directed edge, flagging the ambiguity is part of the adopted approach, not a failure to produce a required direction.
What does the 96% figure contribute to the decision?

It speaks to that abstention behavior: SignalSep flagged 96% of indistinguishable edges in the reported assessment. The figure concerns indistinguishable edges, not all candidate edges. It supports adopting a method that can withhold directional claims where the observations do not separate signaling from an alternative explanation.
Should I describe those flagged edges as environmental effects instead?

No. Flagging an indistinguishable edge means the directed-signaling and environmental explanations cannot be separated on the available basis. It does not establish that the environment caused the observed pattern, or that signaling did not occur.
Are the 84% and 96% figures measuring the same kind of success?

They measure complementary behaviors, not the same quantity. The 84% is precision at 50% recall for directed-edge recovery; the 96% is the proportion of indistinguishable edges flagged. One concerns the correctness of reported edges at a specified recall point, and the other concerns restraint when a directed edge cannot be identified.
Can we say that adopting SignalSep removes the identifiability problem?

No. Abstention is a way to respect that problem, not eliminate it. The decision is to use SignalSep while leaving observationally indistinguishable directed edges flagged. It should not be presented as a way to determine the true direction in cases where the observations cannot do so.
Does clearing the target mean SignalSep has established directed signaling in every tissue?

No. The target-clearing comparison rests on the reported NicheMix-1 precision at 50% recall. It supports the adoption decision as stated, but it does not extend that numerical performance claim to every tissue or imply that every candidate edge is identifiable.
Why make abstention part of the decision rather than just noting it as a side result?

Because distinguishing directed signaling from shared-microenvironment effects requires more than reporting correct edges when a distinction is possible. It also requires avoiding an unwarranted direction when the explanations are observationally indistinguishable. The decision explicitly keeps that flagging behavior alongside the target-clearing recovery result.
Is an abstained edge the same as an incorrect edge?

No. An abstained edge is one on which SignalSep withholds an identified directional claim. That is different from reporting a direction that proves incorrect. For an indistinguishable edge, abstention communicates the limit of the inference rather than choosing between explanations without a basis for doing so.
Could I summarize the decision as ‘84% accuracy and 96% uncertainty detection’?

That would blur both measures. The first number is 84% *precision at 50% recall*, not overall accuracy. The second is that 96% of *indistinguishable edges* were flagged, not a general uncertainty-detection rate. Keeping those terms and denominators makes the reason for adoption clear.
What is the shortest careful statement of the decision?
Adopt SignalSep with abstention: its 84% precision at 50% recall clears the ≥80% target, and it flags 96% of indistinguishable edges instead of asserting an unidentifiable direction.
What should we do next for SignalSep?

Document SignalSep’s niche-independent ligand variation and receptor-specificity assumptions, then validate its ambiguity flags and its precision at 50% recall on NicheMix-2. The precision criterion for that validation is at least 80% for identifiable directed signaling edges. This is a plan for NicheMix-2, not a claim that those checks have already been completed.
What needs to be documented about niche-independent ligand variation?

The documentation should make clear what SignalSep assumes when it uses variation in a sender’s ligand to distinguish a directed effect from a shared-niche explanation. In particular, it should state what it means for the variation relevant to a directional claim to be separable from niche variation. If ligand and niche patterns cannot be distinguished in the observations, the documentation should not imply that the ligand pattern alone identifies signaling.
Does that assumption say the sender’s ligand must be entirely unaffected by the niche?

Seed the sweep with false edges exposed by reweighting, then compare ambiguity sensitivity. This is an activity designed to evaluate the hypothesis, not a finding that underflagging occurs throughout the sweep.
What is being swept—the strength of ligand expression or the strength of detection dependence?

The specified sweep is over niche-dependent *ligand detection*. The ≥2-fold condition refers to detection’s dependence on the niche, not a twofold change in ligand expression or in the number of directed edges. The activity does not give the individual sweep points or an exact detection rule.
Does ≥2-fold mean we only need to examine exactly twofold detection?

No. It includes twofold and greater niche-dependent detection. The activity calls for a sweep in that range, but it does not specify how far above twofold to go or how densely to sample it. Nor does it establish that twofold is already a proven boundary for underflagging.
What does it mean to calibrate the sweep against NicheMix-2 truth?

It means using the NicheMix-2 simulation truth as a reference when assessing the sweep, so apparent edges and ambiguity flags are not judged solely from SignalSep’s own outputs. The activity does not specify a calibration formula or claim that having simulation truth makes every edge identifiable from the observations available to SignalSep.
Why include the MNAR baseline as well?

It gives the niche-detection sweep a baseline from the setting with ligand- and niche-dependent detection. Comparing against it helps frame whether ambiguity sensitivity changes across the proposed detection conditions. The activity does not state a numerical baseline value for ambiguity sensitivity or prescribe how that comparison must be calculated.
Is the purpose to repeat the earlier precision measurements?

The stated focus here is comparing *ambiguity sensitivity*: whether apparent directed edges that warrant ambiguity flags are recognized as such. NicheMix-2 truth and the MNAR baseline serve as references for that assessment. The activity does not specify a new precision result or say that precision is the measure to compare in this sweep.
What does ‘seed reweighting-exposed false edges’ mean?

It means include false-edge cases exposed through the reweighting comparison as cases for the sweep to assess. They are relevant challenges for an observational-equivalence check because a detection-shaped pattern supported an apparent directed claim. ‘Seed’ here does not mean relabeling those edges as true signaling or assuming that every other candidate has the same failure mode.
Why use those cases instead of relying only on newly appearing edges in the sweep?

They provide cases already identified as problematic for directed-edge interpretation under a detection-related comparison. Including them lets the sweep ask whether SignalSep flags ambiguity for that kind of apparent edge as niche-dependent detection varies. The activity does not require that these be the only cases assessed.
What should ‘ambiguity sensitivity’ mean in this comparison?

It concerns how readily the ambiguity assessment flags apparent directed edges that should not be treated as identifiable because a competing explanation remains. For this activity, the question is whether SignalSep recognizes environmental mimics, including the seeded false-edge cases, across the detection sweep. No exact denominator, scoring formula, or required sensitivity threshold is specified.
Could SignalSep simply abstain on every candidate and appear sensitive to ambiguity?

Broad abstention would not, by itself, establish that the checks distinguish ambiguous cases from identifiable directed edges. The comparison should be interpreted as sensitivity to *relevant* ambiguity, not merely a count of flags. This activity names ambiguity sensitivity as the quantity to compare but does not supply a complete scoring protocol.
Where do the matched negative controls in the hypothesis fit?

The hypothesis contrasts SignalSep’s flagging with ambiguity revealed by matched negative controls. This activity specifies a calibrated detection sweep, the NicheMix-2 truth and MNAR baseline references, and seeded reweighting-exposed false edges for comparing ambiguity sensitivity. It does not spell out a new matching procedure or state a result for the controls, so those details should remain open.
If a seeded false edge receives an ambiguity flag, does that establish what caused the original observed pattern?

No. A flag indicates that the apparent direction should not be treated as identified when a competing explanation cannot be distinguished. Even with simulation truth as an assessment reference, SignalSep’s flag is about the limits of inference from its observations; it is not, by itself, a causal diagnosis of the pattern.
Would one detection level with low ambiguity sensitivity confirm the whole ≥2-fold hypothesis?

Not the whole hypothesis. The proposed sweep is meant to compare behavior across the ≥2-fold niche-detection conditions, with the stated references and seeded cases. An outcome at one level would need to retain that level’s scope; it would not establish what happens at every level in the range or settle the predicted contrast with matched negative controls on its own.
What if ambiguity sensitivity varies across the sweep?

That variation would be part of what the activity is designed to reveal. It could help locate where SignalSep flags apparent directed edges and where it underflags them, if the comparison supports those judgments. No pattern of variation is stated in advance, and the ≥2-fold condition should remain a hypothesis being evaluated rather than an assumed cutoff.
Can you state the activity concisely without implying it has produced results?

Calibrate a ≥2-fold niche-dependent ligand-detection sweep against NicheMix-2 simulation truth and the MNAR baseline, include reweighting-exposed false edges, and compare SignalSep’s ambiguity sensitivity. The comparison tests the proposed underflagging regime; its outcome is not yet stated.
What did the niche-dependent detection sweep find about ambiguity flagging?

At 2–4-fold niche-dependent ligand detection, reweighted SignalSep flagged 43% of environmental mimics as ambiguous. With matched controls, ambiguity detection rose to 88%. The contrast shows that reweighting alone left many environmental mimics unflagged in this tested range, while the matched-control comparison revealed substantially more ambiguity.
How large is the difference between 43% and 88%?

It is 45 percentage points. Both figures concern ambiguity detection in the reported 2–4-fold niche-dependent detection range, but they describe different assessments: reweighted SignalSep’s flagging and ambiguity detection with matched controls.
Does 43% mean SignalSep made false directed-edge calls on the other 57%?

Not necessarily. The result says reweighted SignalSep flagged 43% of environmental mimics. It does not specify the output for every unflagged mimic. We can say the remaining 57% were not flagged in that assessment, but we cannot automatically classify all of them as reported directed edges.
Then what exactly is the limitation shown by the 43% figure?

Reweighting did not lead SignalSep to recognize ambiguity for most of the environmental mimics assessed at 2–4-fold niche-dependent detection. That is a limitation of its ambiguity flagging in this condition. The figure is not, by itself, a precision measure or a count of false-edge calls.
What does it mean that matched controls ‘raised ambiguity detection’ to 88%?

It means that including the matched-control comparison exposed ambiguity in a larger share of the assessed cases: 88%, compared with the 43% flagged by reweighted SignalSep. The wording attributes the higher ambiguity-detection result to the comparison with matched controls; it should not be recast as 88% flagging by reweighted SignalSep on its own.
Can I say the controls identified which niche factor caused each mimic?

No. Revealing ambiguity means showing that an apparent directed claim cannot be distinguished from a competing explanation on the available basis. It does not identify a particular niche factor as the cause of every mimic, nor does it establish that signaling was absent in every case.
Is 88% a precision score for the edges that remained after the controls were used?

No. The 88% is an ambiguity-detection figure, not directed-edge precision. This result does not report precision at a particular recall level or describe a set of edges remaining after the matched-control comparison.
Does the result show that propensity reweighting did nothing?

No. It reports how reweighted SignalSep performed on ambiguity flagging—43% of environmental mimics in the 2–4-fold range—but gives no unreweighted ambiguity-flagging figure for this same comparison. The supported conclusion is that reweighting alone did not flag most of those mimics, not that reweighting had zero effect.
Does this establish that exactly twofold niche-dependent detection is the point where the checks fail?
No. The finding covers a 2–4-fold range. It does not isolate an exact transition at twofold, give a result for every individual point in that range, or establish what happens below twofold.
What about niche-dependent detection above fourfold?
No result above fourfold is stated here. The 43% and 88% findings should remain tied to the reported 2–4-fold range rather than being extended to stronger detection dependence.
Should I call this a two- to fourfold change in ligand expression?

No. The condition is 2–4-fold *niche-dependent detection* of the ligand, not a two- to fourfold change in ligand expression. Keeping that distinction matters because the concern is that the observation process can make an apparent signaling pattern misleading.
Could strong receptor linkage override the ambiguity revealed by the controls?

The reported finding does not establish that it could. A receptor-linked pattern can motivate a signaling explanation, but the matched-control result concerns whether an environmental mimic remains a competing explanation. If that ambiguity is revealed, receptor linkage alone should not be described as having identified a direction in those cases.
Is the gap between the two figures evidence about edge recovery?

It is evidence about *ambiguity detection*, not a reported edge-recovery measure. The 45-percentage-point gap shows that the matched-control comparison revealed ambiguity more often than reweighted SignalSep flagged environmental mimics in this range. It does not tell us the recall or precision of directed edges in the sweep.
Does an environmental mimic necessarily have a true directed signaling edge underneath it?

The label concerns an apparent signaling pattern for which an environmental explanation is relevant. This finding does not state the underlying status of each assessed candidate. The point of the figures is whether ambiguity was flagged or revealed, not a declaration that every mimic contains—or lacks—a true directed edge.
How carefully should I describe the comparison without turning it into a broader claim about SignalSep?

Keep the condition, measures, and comparison together: at 2–4-fold niche-dependent ligand detection, reweighted SignalSep flagged 43% of environmental mimics, while matched controls raised ambiguity detection to 88%. That identifies underflagging in this assessment and the added ambiguity revealed by matched controls; it does not provide a universal dropout threshold, an edge-precision result, or a finding for other detection ranges.
How can we test whether the proposed ≥2-fold detection-bias boundary holds beyond the cases used to formulate it?

Why choose 1.5-fold as well as 2- and 3-fold?

The three specified levels let the comparison include one condition below the hypothesized ≥2-fold boundary, one at it, and one above it. That can probe whether the predicted difference between reweighted and matched-control flags appears around those tested levels. It does not make 2-fold an established cutoff or determine what happens at untested values.
What does ‘held-out’ contribute to the test?

It means the comparison is to be made on NicheMix-MNAR tissues set aside for this test, rather than treating the cases used to develop the hypothesis as the test itself. The activity does not specify how the tissues were held out, how many there are, or what outcomes they contain.
Are the three levels percentages of dropout?

No. They are fold levels of detection bias: 1.5-, 2-, and 3-fold. They should not be converted into percentages of missing ligand observations. The activity does not provide a dropout percentage or a formula relating these bias levels to one.
Should I describe the bias as ligand–niche-dependent detection?

NicheMix-MNAR is the stated tissue setting, and the proposed hypothesis concerns niche-dependent ligand detection. The activity specifies detection-bias levels in that setting. What outputs are being compared at each bias level?

The specified outputs are ambiguity flags after reweighting and ambiguity flags from the matched-control comparison. The question is whether they agree about which apparent directed edges should be treated as ambiguous, or whether the matched controls reveal ambiguity that the reweighted assessment does not flag. The activity supplies no comparison results yet.
Does ‘reweighted ambiguity flags’ mean we reweight the flags themselves?

It is better read as ambiguity flags produced in the reweighted assessment, not as numerical weights applied to preexisting flags. The activity names reweighting as part of one side of the comparison, but does not prescribe a weighting formula or a procedure for generating the flags.
And are matched-control flags a declaration that the niche definitely caused each response?

No. A matched-control ambiguity flag concerns whether a directed signaling interpretation remains distinguishable from an alternative in the comparison. It should not be interpreted as proof that a niche caused the response, or that signaling is absent.
If both approaches flag an apparent edge, what could we conclude?

They would agree in flagging that edge as ambiguous in the tested condition. Such agreement would be about withholding an identified directional claim, not about identifying the underlying cause. The activity does not say whether this agreement occurs at any of the three bias levels.
What if only the matched-control comparison flags it?

That would be the kind of disagreement relevant to the underflagging hypothesis: the reweighted assessment would not have flagged ambiguity that the matched-control comparison reveals. It would still be necessary to interpret what each flag means under the stated assumptions; the activity does not report any such disagreement as an observed result.
Could reweighted SignalSep flag an edge that the matched controls do not?

That is another possible comparison outcome. A disagreement in that direction should not automatically be labeled a mistake by either side without examining the basis for the flags. The test asks for a comparison; it does not say matched controls are infallible or supply an adjudication rule for every disagreement.
If the flags differ at 2-fold but not 1.5-fold, can we declare a sharp threshold?

Not on that contrast alone. What would the 3-fold condition add to that interpretation?

It supplies a second tested level above the proposed boundary. Comparing flags at 3-fold with those at 2-fold could show whether a pattern seen at the boundary also appears at that higher tested level. It would not establish the pattern for every bias greater than or equal to 2-fold.
Is this test measuring directed-edge precision at 50% recall?

That is not the stated comparison. The activity specifies reweighted ambiguity flags versus matched-control flags on held-out NicheMix-MNAR tissues at three detection-bias levels. It gives no precision-at-50%-recall result or instruction to calculate one as part of this particular test.
Does a greater number of flags automatically mean better ambiguity detection?

No. A count alone cannot distinguish appropriate flags from indiscriminate abstention. The relevant comparison concerns which apparent directed claims each approach marks ambiguous at each stated bias level. The activity does not define a numerical success threshold for the comparison.
Could we treat an unflagged edge as confirmed signaling?

No. The absence of an ambiguity flag is an output of a check, not independent proof that the directed interpretation is correct or identifiable. Should the three bias levels be pooled into one overall comparison?

The plan specifies testing at 1.5-, 2-, and 3-fold detection bias, so results should retain which condition they came from. An aggregate alone could hide whether the flag comparison changes below, at, or above the proposed boundary. No pooling rule is specified.
Can the matched controls establish that reweighting never works?

No. This test compares flags at three specified bias levels in held-out NicheMix-MNAR tissues. A difference in flags at a tested level would speak to that comparison, not prove that reweighting has no value in all settings or for all candidate edges.
How should I describe the test without claiming that the held-out tissues already support the hypothesis?

Say: test held-out NicheMix-MNAR tissues at 1.5-, 2-, and 3-fold detection bias, comparing ambiguity flags from the reweighted assessment with matched-control flags at each level. The purpose is to evaluate the proposed ≥2-fold underflagging pattern; the held-out flag comparisons and any conclusions from them remain to be determined.
What did the held-out NicheMix-MNAR test show at 3-fold detection bias?

At 3-fold detection bias, reweighted SignalSep flagged 91% of environmental mimics as ambiguous, versus 87% for the matched controls. Reweighted SignalSep’s flagging rate was four percentage points higher in this held-out condition.
Does that mean the matched controls found more ambiguity than reweighted SignalSep?

No. At this tested level, the reported percentages go the other way: 91% for reweighted SignalSep and 87% for matched controls. The figures concern ambiguity flagging of environmental mimics, not the precision of directed-edge calls.
Is four percentage points the same as saying SignalSep found four more ambiguous edges?
No. Four percentage points is the difference between the reported percentages. Without the number of environmental mimics assessed, it cannot be converted into a count of edges.
Can we tell whether the two approaches flagged exactly the same mimics?

No. The percentages give aggregate flagging rates, not the identities of the flagged candidates. Both approaches could have flagged many of the same mimics, or their flags could differ on particular cases; that overlap is not stated.
What does an ambiguity flag tell us about an environmental mimic?

It tells us that the apparent directed edge was flagged as ambiguous rather than treated as an identified direction. The flag does not, by itself, determine what caused the observed pattern or prove that signaling was absent.
Does the 91% figure mean 91% of all apparent edges in those tissues were flagged?
No. Its stated denominator is environmental mimics in the held-out NicheMix-MNAR condition at 3-fold bias. It should not be generalized to all apparent edges or all cells in those tissues.
What can we say about the environmental mimics SignalSep did not flag?

The 91% figure leaves 9% of environmental mimics unflagged by reweighted SignalSep in this assessment. The finding does not say whether those candidates received directed-edge calls or some other output, so it would be unwarranted to count all of them as false directed calls.
Does the matched controls’ 87% mean they resolved the true cause for 87% of the mimics?

No. It is an ambiguity-flagging percentage. Flagging a mimic as ambiguous means a directed explanation is not being treated as uniquely identified; it is not a causal identification of the niche or any other specific source.
Can this result establish a detection-bias threshold at exactly 3-fold?
No. It reports flagging at one tested level, 3-fold detection bias. It does not locate a transition point or establish how flagging behaves at levels between the tested values.
The held-out test included other bias levels. Do we know their outcomes from this finding?

Could I say reweighting guarantees better ambiguity detection than matched controls whenever niche-dependent detection is at least twofold?

No. The observed four-percentage-point difference is specific to held-out NicheMix-MNAR at 3-fold bias. It neither guarantees the same ordering at other bias levels nor establishes that reweighting will flag every environmental mimic.
Does this finding tell us whether directed-edge precision met a target?
No precision or recall figure is reported here. The finding compares ambiguity flags for environmental mimics. It should not be converted into a claim about directed-edge precision at 50% recall.
What is the most careful short statement of the result?

On held-out NicheMix-MNAR tissues at 3-fold detection bias, reweighted SignalSep flagged 91% of environmental mimics as ambiguous, compared with 87% for matched controls. The result describes that condition’s aggregate flagging rates, not edge precision or outcomes at other bias levels.
When do reciprocal ligand–receptor interactions make edge direction unidentifiable from cross-sectional spatial transcriptomics?

They make direction unidentifiable when the observed ligand–receptor patterns are compatible with more than one directional account and the available observations and assumptions cannot distinguish those accounts. If each neighboring cell could plausibly act as both sender and receiver, a single spatial snapshot may not tell us which directed influence, if either, produced the observed responses. That is the identifiability question; reciprocity alone does not establish that every edge is unidentifiable.
What does reciprocal mean in this question?

It means that a ligand–receptor interpretation is plausible in both directions between the cells: each may have a candidate way to send a signal to the other. The question is not merely whether the cells are associated. It asks whether the observations can distinguish one sender-to-receiver claim from its reverse or from a genuinely two-way interpretation.
If there is a plausible interaction in each direction, shouldn't we just report two directed edges?

Only if each direction is identifiable on the available basis. Two plausible ligand–receptor accounts are not the same as evidence that both directed influences occurred. A one-way account, a two-way account, or another explanation might fit the cross-sectional observations. Reporting two identified edges would overstate the evidence if those possibilities remain observationally indistinguishable.
Could we instead choose whichever direction has the stronger observed ligand pattern?

A stronger observed pattern does not necessarily identify the direction of influence. It might make one account look more compatible with the snapshot, but direction requires a basis for distinguishing that account from the reverse and from other relevant explanations. The question supplies no rule under which relative pattern strength settles that distinction.
Why does the data being cross-sectional matter?

Cross-sectional data describe the cells in a spatial snapshot rather than showing the order in which their states changed. If both directions are compatible with what is observed at that snapshot, the observations alone do not establish which cell acted first or which influence produced the other cell’s state. That does not mean direction can never be identified from cross-sectional data; it means any directional claim needs an explicit distinguishing basis.
Is the problem simply that we cannot tell which cell expressed its ligand first?

That is one way to see the temporal ambiguity, but the issue is broader. Even without asking which event came first, we need to know whether the available observations discriminate an influence from cell A to cell B from an influence from B to A, from both influences, or from a shared influence on the cells. The question is about identifying directed edges, not just reconstructing an order of ligand expression.
Suppose both cells show a ligand and a corresponding receptor. Does that prove the interaction was reciprocal?

No. It supplies patterns compatible with reciprocal signaling, but observing the components is not the same as observing both influences take place. The patterns could also be compatible with fewer directed influences or with an explanation that does not establish either direction. The question asks when those alternatives cannot be distinguished from the cross-sectional observations.
What if each cell also shows a response compatible with the other's ligand?

That makes a two-way account plausible, but it still does not automatically identify two directed edges. Each observed response would have to be distinguishable from explanations that do not require the proposed incoming signal. If the same snapshot fits one-way, two-way, and shared-environment accounts under the relevant assumptions, the separate directions remain unidentifiable.
Are we asking whether reciprocity makes the existence of any interaction uncertain, or specifically whether it makes direction uncertain?

Specifically, the question concerns edge direction. An observed pattern could motivate a candidate interaction while leaving it unresolved whether influence ran one way, the other way, or both ways. Conversely, uncertainty about whether any signaling occurred may coexist with the directional ambiguity. Those are related but distinct limits on inference.
If both directions really occur, isn't labeling direction ‘unidentifiable’ misleading?

Not if the label describes what can be inferred from the observations rather than what happens in the underlying tissue. Both directions could occur, yet a cross-sectional snapshot might not distinguish that account from a one-way or non-signaling explanation. ‘Unidentifiable’ says the available basis cannot establish the proposed directed claim; it does not say the claim is false.
How does the shared microenvironment enter a question about reciprocal interactions?

A shared microenvironment may affect both neighboring cells and produce patterns that look compatible with their influencing each other. Reciprocity adds possible directions to compare, while the environmental explanation adds another possible source of their related states. A directional claim must remain distinguishable from these relevant alternatives; observing compatible ligand–receptor patterns in both cells does not, by itself, remove the shared-environment possibility.
Does incomplete molecular observation matter here too?

Yes. If some relevant molecular information is unobserved, the apparent support for one direction over the other may be incomplete or misleading. Missing observations cannot be treated as evidence that the corresponding signaling possibility is absent. The extent of the problem depends on which distinctions the available observations and stated assumptions actually support; incomplete observation does not automatically decide the question for every pair.
Would finding an asymmetry in the observed profiles be enough to orient the edge?

It could be relevant, but asymmetry by itself is not a guarantee of an identifiable direction. The asymmetry must provide information that separates the proposed influence from its reverse and from relevant shared-environment explanations under explicit assumptions. Otherwise it is a difference in observed profiles, not necessarily an identified sender-to-receiver edge.
Is observational equivalence possible between one-way and two-way signaling, not just between signaling and environment?

Yes, that is part of the question. If the cross-sectional observations do not distinguish an A-to-B effect from a B-to-A effect or from both together, those directional accounts are observationally equivalent for the inference at hand. A check focused only on whether *some* ligand–receptor account fits would miss that ambiguity about the individual directed edges.
Can SignalSep's observational-equivalence checks settle this just because they are included in the model?

Their inclusion does not guarantee that the snapshot contains enough information to orient reciprocal candidate interactions. The checks would need to assess whether the competing directional accounts are distinguishable under SignalSep’s assumptions. If they are not, the appropriate response for an unidentifiable directed edge is abstention, rather than treating the presence of a check as proof that one direction has been established.
If SignalSep abstains on a reciprocal candidate, should we describe the cells as having no relationship?

No. Abstention on direction is narrower than a conclusion that no relationship exists. It leaves open the possibilities of one-way signaling, two-way signaling, or an explanation involving their shared environment when the available observations cannot discriminate among them. The point is not to erase the observed pattern, but to avoid assigning it an unsupported direction.
What would a careful answer to the original question look like without assuming that every reciprocal case has the same outcome?

Reciprocal ligand–receptor interactions make edge direction unidentifiable from cross-sectional spatial transcriptomics when the observed patterns and explicit assumptions cannot distinguish the individual directions from each other, from a two-way account, or from relevant shared-environment explanations. Reciprocity creates candidate explanations, not an automatic verdict: if a particular direction has a defensible distinguishing basis, it may be identified; otherwise its ambiguity should be flagged rather than reported as an established directed edge.
How should we investigate whether reciprocal ligand–receptor interactions leave edge direction unidentifiable?

What is meant by reciprocal feedback here?

It is a simulated setting in which influence can run between cells in both directions. Does ‘twin’ mean the two simulations have identical observed data?

Are reciprocal feedback and reversed-edge twins the same test?

They are related but distinct challenges named in the activity. What specifically should directional abstention mean in this test?

It means SignalSep withholds an identified sender-to-receiver direction when the available observations cannot distinguish the relevant directional accounts. Could SignalSep abstain on one direction while identifying the other?

That is conceptually possible if the observations and assumptions support one directional claim but not the other. The activity does not prescribe such an outcome. Would simply making many abstentions show that the test succeeded?

No. Abstaining on every candidate would not show that SignalSep recognizes which directions are actually unidentifiable. If SignalSep favors one direction in a reversed-edge pair, does that settle the identifiability question?

The test should preserve the distinction between recovering simulated truth and appropriately withholding an unidentifiable direction.

Yes. Calibrating to environmental-mimic flag rates keeps that ambiguity relevant, while the new simulations focus on reciprocal and reversed directional accounts. An apparent ligand–receptor pattern might require distinguishing direction from its reverse, from feedback in both directions, and from a shared-environment explanation. No. The stated activity is to calibrate dropout to the observed 43% and 91% mimic-flag rates and simulate reciprocal feedback and reversed-edge twins to test directional abstention. It gives no new precision target, recall point, or outcome for the reciprocal cases.
